items.stem: Which country introduced a lifetime income-tax exemption for mothers of four or more children in 2020?
items.answer: Hungary
items.markingKey: Hungary. Hungary's family policy is one of the most generous pro-natalist packages in Europe.

items.stem: Explain why governments with ageing populations may encourage immigration.
items.answer: Young migrants add workers and taxpayers, fill care and health shortages and slow the rise in old-age dependency, e.g. Japan's Specified Skilled Worker visa (2019) and Germany's Skilled Immigration Act (2020).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Young migrants add workers and taxpayers, fill care and health shortages and slow the rise in old-age dependency, e.g. Japan's Specified Skilled Worker visa (2019) and Germany's Skilled Immigration Act (2020). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between incentive-based population policies and coercive population policies.
items.answer: Coercive policies use legal force or penalties (India's 1975-77 forced sterilisation, China's fines and forced abortions); incentive-based policies rely on voluntary rewards and services.
items.markingKey: Coercive policies use legal force or penalties (India's 1975-77 forced sterilisation, China's fines and forced abortions); incentive-based policies rely on voluntary rewards and services. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Refer to the data below.

Graph description: China's population peaked at about 1.412 billion in 2021 and fell to about 1.409 billion in 2023; births fell from 17.9 million (2016) to 9.0 million (2023).

Suggest why births fell despite the two- and three-child policies.
items.answer: High costs of housing and education, delayed marriage, smaller cohorts of women aged 20-35 (a legacy of the one-child era), changing attitudes and the COVID-19 period.
items.markingKey: High costs of housing and education, delayed marriage, smaller cohorts of women aged 20-35 (a legacy of the one-child era), changing attitudes and the COVID-19 period. items.stem: Briefly describe Japan and explain what it reveals about policies for an ageing population.
items.answer: Combines childcare expansion (Angel Plan 1994) with raising pension ages, robotics in care and new migrant worker visas (2019) Japan uses a mix of pro-natalist, labour and immigration measures to manage population decline.
items.markingKey: Context (Combines childcare expansion (Angel Plan 1994) with raising pension ages, robotics in care and new migrant worker visas (2019)) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Evaluate the claim that population policies are rarely effective in changing fertility rates.
items.answer: Policies work best when aligned with social change; they can speed decline more easily than they can reverse it.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - for: pro-natalist incentives in Singapore, South Korea and Japan have had little effect; fertility often fell before policies started. Against / limitations: China and Iran show policy can accelerate change; France's long-term family policy helps sustain TFR near 1.7-1.8. A supported conclusion might be: Policies work best when aligned with social change; they can speed decline more easily than they can reverse it. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "pro-natalist policy"?
options: The economic growth potential that arises when the working-age share of a population is large relative to dependants, following a fall in fertility
A government policy that aims to increase birth rates, e.g. through child benefits, tax breaks, parental leave and childcare
A cultural preference for male children, which can lead to sex-selective abortion and neglect of girls
Formal or informal marriage before the age of 18, strongly linked to early childbearing and high fertility
items.answer: A government policy that aims to increase birth rates, e.g. through child benefits, tax breaks, parental leave and childcare
items.markingKey: B. "pro-natalist policy" is a government policy that aims to increase birth rates, e.g. through child benefits, tax breaks, parental leave and childcare.

items.stem: Explain why pro-natalist policies often have only a small effect on fertility.
items.answer: Incentives are small relative to the lifetime cost of a child; fertility decisions reflect housing costs, women's careers, work culture and gender roles, which cash benefits do not change - e.g. Singapore's TFR stays near 1.0 despite the Baby Bonus.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Incentives are small relative to the lifetime cost of a child; fertility decisions reflect housing costs, women's careers, work culture and gender roles, which cash benefits do not change - e.g. Singapore's TFR stays near 1.0 despite the Baby Bonus. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Ingrid writes: "Raising the pension age is a pro-natalist policy." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: It is an ageing policy that keeps people in work longer; it does not aim to raise births.
items.markingKey: It is an ageing policy that keeps people in work longer; it does not aim to raise births. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

Using a named example, outline one success and one problem of an anti-natalist policy.
items.answer: e.g. China: success - an estimated 400 million fewer births (government claim) and reduced pressure on resources; problem - rapid ageing, labour shortages and a sex ratio imbalance.

items.stem: "China's one-child policy did more harm than good." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: It contributed to development but at serious social and human-rights cost, with lasting demographic problems.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "child marriage"?
options: Equal rights, responsibilities and opportunities for women and men, girls and boys
A set of government measures designed to influence the size, growth, structure or distribution of a population
Policies that control the number and type of migrants to meet labour-market and demographic needs
Formal or informal marriage before the age of 18, strongly linked to early childbearing and high fertility
items.answer: Formal or informal marriage before the age of 18, strongly linked to early childbearing and high fertility
items.markingKey: D. "child marriage" is formal or informal marriage before the age of 18, strongly linked to early childbearing and high fertility.

items.stem: Jonas writes: "Gender equality is only a social issue, not a population issue." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Women's education, empowerment and reproductive rights are among the most powerful influences on fertility, mortality and population growth.
items.markingKey: Women's education, empowerment and reproductive rights are among the most powerful influences on fertility, mortality and population growth. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between female literacy and female labour-force participation.
items.answer: Literacy measures women's ability to read and write, an outcome of schooling; labour-force participation measures the share of women working or seeking work, linked to income and autonomy.
items.markingKey: Literacy measures women's ability to read and write, an outcome of schooling; labour-force participation measures the share of women working or seeking work, linked to income and autonomy. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.answer: Enforcing a minimum marriage age of 18, cash transfers conditional on girls staying in school, community awareness campaigns with religious leaders.

items.answer: Female education is arguably the most powerful long-term factor, but it works through and alongside health, contraception and economic change.

items.stem: Explain how son preference can distort population structure.
items.answer: Sex-selective abortion and neglect of daughters produce more boys than girls, leading to "surplus" men who cannot find marriage partners, e.g. China and northern India.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Sex-selective abortion and neglect of daughters produce more boys than girls, leading to "surplus" men who cannot find marriage partners, e.g. China and northern India. items.stem: Explain why gender inequality can contribute to high population growth.
items.answer: Where women lack education, income and autonomy, early marriage and pressure to have sons persist and access to contraception is limited, keeping fertility high (e.g. Niger, where most girls marry before 18).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Where women lack education, income and autonomy, early marriage and pressure to have sons persist and access to contraception is limited, keeping fertility high (e.g. Niger, where most girls marry before 18). Explain one way the rise in girls' schooling could have contributed to this change.
items.answer: Girls stayed in school longer, delaying marriage and first births; educated women used contraception more and had paid employment opportunities (e.g. garment industry).

items.stem: Outline one way in which Bangladesh shows the role of women's empowerment in fertility decline.
items.answer: TFR fell from about 6.3 to around 2.0 through community family-planning workers and girls' school stipends. Improved schooling and contraception access for women drove one of the fastest declines in South Asia.
items.markingKey: Context (TFR fell from about 6.3 to around 2.0 through community family-planning workers and girls' school stipends.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.answer: (a) Generally negative: countries with more female schooling have lower TFR; Niger and Mali (low schooling) have the highest fertility; Nigeria is an exception with higher schooling but high TFR. (b) Nigeria's national average hides strong regional contrasts (higher schooling in the south, low in the north); cultural and religious norms, child marriage and limited contraception access also matter.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "demographic dividend".
items.answer: The economic growth potential that arises when the working-age share of a population is large relative to dependants, following a fall in fertility

items.stem: Briefly explain why a demographic dividend is not automatic.
items.answer: The larger working-age population boosts growth only if there are jobs, education and health, good governance, savings and investment; without them a "youth bulge" can bring unemployment and unrest.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The larger working-age population boosts growth only if there are jobs, education and health, good governance, savings and investment; without them a "youth bulge" can bring unemployment and unrest. items.stem: Explain the difference between a temporary guest-worker programme and a points-based system.
items.answer: A points system selects permanent migrants by skills and attributes; guest-worker programmes admit temporary workers for specific jobs, often without a path to settlement (e.g. Gulf kafala, Germany's 1960s Gastarbeiter).
items.markingKey: A points system selects permanent migrants by skills and attributes; guest-worker programmes admit temporary workers for specific jobs, often without a path to settlement (e.g. Gulf kafala, Germany's 1960s Gastarbeiter). items.answer: Its working-age population has shrunk since the mid-1990s and care, construction and agriculture face severe labour shortages; ageing raised dependency.
items.markingKey: Its working-age population has shrunk since the mid-1990s and care, construction and agriculture face severe labour shortages; ageing raised dependency.

items.stem: Outline one argument for and one argument against the view that countries with youthful populations in sub-Saharan Africa are likely to gain a demographic dividend.
items.answer: A dividend is possible but not guaranteed; it depends on rapid fertility decline and investment in skills and jobs.
items.markingKey: For: fertility is falling in many countries (Kenya, Ethiopia, Rwanda). Against: fertility decline is slow and has stalled in some countries. items.stem: Which agreement removed internal border controls between many European countries?
items.answer: The Schengen Agreement
items.markingKey: C. The Schengen Area allows passport-free travel across 29 European countries.

items.stem: Elena writes: "A demographic dividend lasts indefinitely." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: It is temporary: as the large working-age cohorts age, the old-age dependency ratio rises (as in Japan and now China).
items.markingKey: It is temporary: as the large working-age cohorts age, the old-age dependency ratio rises (as in Japan and now China). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a demographic dividend and a youth bulge.
items.answer: A dividend is the growth gained when a large working-age population is productively employed; a youth bulge is a large share of young people that can bring unemployment and instability if jobs are lacking.
items.markingKey: A dividend is the growth gained when a large working-age population is productively employed; a youth bulge is a large share of young people that can bring unemployment and instability if jobs are lacking. items.answer: net migration +13.2 per 1,000; total change +11.9 per 1,000; dominant component: migration

items.stem: Examine the view that selective immigration policies are the best response to an ageing population.
items.answer: Immigration helps but is best combined with labour participation, productivity and pension reforms.

items.stem: Explain how female employment can increase the size of a demographic dividend.

items.stem:
Study the infographic / visual stimulus described below.

Table: total fertility rate, Singapore - 1960: 5.8; 1975: 2.1; 1987: 1.6; 2001: 1.4; 2023: 0.97.

(a) Describe the trend in TFR in relation to Singapore's population policies. [4]
(b) Using the resource and your own knowledge, calculate the percentage change in TFR between 1987 and 2023. [6]
items.answer: (a) TFR fell rapidly to replacement by 1975 (Stop at Two, 1972) and kept falling; after pro-natalist policies (1987) and the Baby Bonus (2001) it continued to decline to below 1.0. (b) (0.97 − 1.6)/1.6 × 100 = -39.4%

items.answer: population policy

items.stem: Explain the difference between pro-natalist policies and anti-natalist policies.
items.answer: Pro-natalist policies try to raise fertility (Singapore Baby Bonus, Hungary tax exemptions); anti-natalist policies try to reduce it (China's one-child policy, Iran's 1989 family planning programme).

items.stem: Explain why the kafala system has been criticised.
items.answer: Tying workers to employers allows abuse - confiscated passports, unpaid wages and inability to change jobs - as reported for migrant workers in Qatar before the 2022 World Cup reforms.

items.stem: "Greater gender equality always raises fertility in high-income countries." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The relationship is not simple: Nordic countries with high equality have TFRs that have also fallen to around 1.4-1.5 since 2010.

items.stem: Felix writes: "Any country with a falling birth rate will automatically become richer." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The dividend requires jobs, investment, education and governance; without them a large working-age population may be unemployed.

items.stem: A population data sheet lists Italy with 8.0 births and 11.6 deaths per 1,000 people per year. Calculate the rate of natural increase (NIR) as a percentage.
items.answer: NIR = (8.0 − 11.6) / 10 = -0.36% per year (natural decrease)
items.markingKey: M1 subtracting CDR from CBR (-3.6 per 1,000); A1 dividing by 10: -0.36%.

items.stem:
The table shows data for a sample of countries from the World Bank database (site: GDP per capita (US$ thousand, PPP), life expectancy at birth (years)).
A: 11.5, 60.3; B: 26.2, 65.6; C: 23.9, 64.0; D: 17.9, 61.4; E: 46.0, 74.7; F: 47.1, 74.4; G: 65.6, 82.8; H: 58.8, 79.1.
Calculate Spearman's rank correlation coefficient (rs = 1 − 6Σd² / (n³ − n)) and state whether the relationship is significant at the 0.05 level (one-tailed test; critical value for n = 8: 0.643).
items.answer: Σd² = 2; rs = 1 − 6×2/(8³ − 8) = 0.976; a positive correlation that is significant at the 0.05 level.
items.markingKey: M1 ranking both variables (rank 1 = highest); M1 d² summed: Σd² = 2; A1 rs = 0.976; R1 |rs| >= 0.643 so reject the null hypothesis.

items.stem: Suggest two measures, other than cash payments, that could raise fertility in South Korea.
items.answer: Affordable housing for young couples, shorter working hours and flexible work, better parental leave uptake by fathers, cheaper education to reduce competitive hagwon costs.

items.stem: "Countries with youthful populations in sub-Saharan Africa are likely to gain a demographic dividend." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: A dividend is possible but not guaranteed; it depends on rapid fertility decline and investment in skills and jobs.
